tier_reason: Public benchmark code benchmarks/flat-rb-tree-benchmark.cpp times dro::FlatMap vs std::map (plus boost/folly); README states gcc 14.2.1, -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, and Intel Core i5-9300H with isolcpus; exact per-size results are committed as text in benchmarks/results/*.txt, so A holds.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Exact means from the repo's benchmarks/results/*.txt (charts in README plot the same data): 10,000,000 int32 elements: insert 622 ns vs std::map 855 ns, find 551 ns vs 774 ns, erase 627 ns vs 916 ns; 1,000,000 elements: insert 283 vs 461 ns, find 234 vs 438 ns, erase 281 vs 470 ns (about 1.4-1.9x, derived from page data). Versus boost::flat_map, insert/erase explode past a few thousand elements (1M: 146,200 ns insert) but boost::flat_map FIND is faster than dro::FlatMap at large sizes (1M: 134 ns vs 234 ns), and folly::heap_vector_map find is faster than dro from ~100K elements up per the find chart.
corrections.caveats: Charts are PNG but exact numbers are in benchmarks/results/*.txt; each size is a single run reporting mean ns/op over the op count with no variance; only one hardware/compiler configuration (libstdc++ via gcc 14.2.1); project is self-described beta (~50% test coverage); the 'faster than boost::flat_map' claim applies to insert/erase only, not find.

notes: Chart readings in the record were close to the committed text results (e.g. 10M find 551 vs 774 ns); corrected to exact values and fixed the overstated boost::flat_map find claim. Metadata verified: GPL-3.0, 14 stars, last commit 2024-11-16 (stale), not a fork.

tier_reason: The ART paper (peer-reviewed) benchmarks the authors' own unreleased ART against their own red-black tree, not libart and not std::map; libart ships no benchmarks at all, so the only numbers are indirect algorithm-level evidence and cannot carry B for this repo (D is arguable if project-specific numbers are required).

corrections.claimed_speedup: From the ART paper's Fig. 10 (single-threaded lookups of random existing 32-bit keys; derived from page data: read off bar chart, approximate; measures the paper authors' ART, not libart): 65K keys: ART ~108M lookups/s dense, ~35M/s sparse vs red-black tree ~7.5M/s (~14x dense, ~4.7x sparse); 16M keys: ART ~20M/s dense, ~10.7M/s sparse vs RB ~1.2M/s (~17x / ~9x); 256M keys: ART ~10.1M/s dense, ~6.8M/s sparse vs RB ~0.65M/s (~15x / ~10x). The paper's chained hash table beats ART on sparse keys at every size; in Fig. 11 (16M keys, 12 threads, 8-way software pipelining) ART dense ~195M/s vs hash table ~132M/s, but ART sparse ~110M/s is slower than the hash table. The paper's 1.6-1.7x (ART) and 1.2x (HT) figures are speedups from software pipelining, not ART-vs-HT ratios.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 836 stars; the ART algorithm (the paper's implementation, not libart) was integrated into the HyPer main-memory database per the paper
corrections.caveats: libart has no benchmarks of its own (repo has only src/ and tests/); all numbers come from the ART paper (ICDE 2013), which measured the authors' own ART and own red-black tree ('two textbook data structures'), not libart and not libstdc++/libc++/MSVC std::map; values are read off bar charts; the paper removed path compression for the 32-bit-key micro-benchmarks; the paper's hash table beats ART on sparse keys; libart last commit 2021-02-11 (abandoned).

notes: Record misread Fig. 10 (the red-black tree is ~7.5M/s at 65K, not 10-15M/s, so the real ratio is larger) and misattributed the 1.2-1.7x software-pipelining speedups as an ART-vs-hash-table win (ART sparse is slower than HT). Downgraded because the evidence is for the algorithm, not this implementation; license verified BSD-3-Clause from LICENSE (GitHub reports NOASSERTION).
